title: Ever buy more than you mean to when shopping online? This could be why
byline: Stephanie Kampf, Daniela Silva, Katie Swyers, Asha Tomlinson

image.caption: Marketplace tracked popular online shopping sites to reveal tactics companies use to influence your behaviour. (Adobe stock)

blocks.text: Ever buy more than you mean to online? It could be by design.
CBC's Marketplace tracked popular online shopping sites Amazon, Shein, Temu and Walmart, revealing the tactics companies use which can influence your behaviour.
Can you trust every sale countdown timer? How about that inventory counter? Not necessarily.

They can be part of what experts call "dark patterns," a type of design on a website or app that can steer you into a decision that might not be in your best interest, and something that can be found across the internet.

"What's spooky about it is that people don't even know it's happening, and so their choices as shoppers are being guided invisibly," said Ryan Fritsch, an advocate for protecting consumers in the digital marketplace and a lawyer for the Law Commission of Ontario.
Ryan Fritsch, lawyer for the Law Commission of Ontario, says dark patterns 'try and trick consumers into making choices that may not be in their interest.' (Will Arnold/CBC)

Marketplace put it to the test in a series of spot checks, tracking sites and apps each week for about a month, and found several pressure tactics. Here’s what to be aware of the next time you're shopping online.
False urgency
The team saw a pair of leggings on Amazon with a stock counter that said only one left, so they bought what appeared to be the last pair. But eight minutes later, they were able to buy a second pair.
A message from Amazon saying we recently ordered what they said was the last pair of leggings, before we ordered a second pair. (CBC)

That second pair shipped a few days later than the first, but Fritsch said, "I think that if they're telling you there's only one left, that should be an honest statement. Otherwise, they are deceiving consumers. It's unfair."
Amazon’s stock count said these leggings were the last pair, but Asha Tomlinson and Ryan Fritsch show two pairs of leggings. (CBC)
Similarly, the Marketplace team saw coupons on Shein with a 24-hour countdown timer. But when the time ran out, the sale simply started over again.
"It's creating a false sense of urgency," said Jacquelyn Burkell, a professor in the faculty of information and media studies at the Western University in London, Ont.
"They're playing you, right?" said Fritsch. "The consumer is being induced to make an impulsive purchase that may not be in their best interest when other, better options might be available to them."
Pre-selected options

Another tactic is pre-selected options, which can also work against a consumer’s best interests. When buying the leggings on Amazon, Marketplace noticed the company had pre-selected slightly faster paid shipping for $7.98 as the default — even though free shipping was an option.
Fritsch said a busy shopper might not even notice.
Paid delivery was a pre-selected option on Amazon Canada, even though free delivery was available. (CBC)
Visual interference

Something else experts say to watch for are bright colours that can draw your eye and lead you into a decision. During checkout, both Walmart and Amazon used bright colours to attract attention to signing up for their membership programs, while the option to decline was on a white background.
A pop-up message on Amazon promoting their membership with a yellow button saying 'Start 30-day FREE trial.' (CBC)
Burkell said "a big bright yellow thing is going to be more evident to you" and "when it attracts attention…you're more likely to act."
Shoppers who Marketplace spoke with at the CBC Broadcast Centre in Toronto agreed.
Trisha Arocena said she’s seen this on Amazon before and "it makes the decision almost easier for you. So you're prompted to go ahead and click."
Ritu Gill said if she’s in a rush, "Your eyes do follow … the bright blue button. 'Let me just click yes, yes, yes, get through this and make the purchase.'"
A pop-up message on Walmart Canada promoting their membership with a blue button saying 'Confirm Plan.' (CBC)

In a statement, a spokesperson for Walmart Canada said the company's goal is to provide customers with a transparent and easy-to-navigate online shopping experience. They said the membership offer is optional and clearly presents consumers with "both the membership option and the option to close the offer and continue with their checkout."
The statement added that Walmart is "committed to complying with applicable laws and regulations."
An Amazon spokesperson said in an email that they "work hard to offer customers a transparent and trustworthy shopping experience."

"When Amazon displays how many units of an item are left in stock, that information reflects inventory on hand and ready to ship with a specific delivery estimate. The Amazon.ca store complies with all applicable Canadian laws, including consumer protection, competition and privacy laws."
Nagging

After the Marketplace team left items in the shopping cart on Temu, the company immediately emailed saying "Action required" and "Complete checkout" with a price drop. Temu continued to email and text about the cart multiple times in the following days.
This type of dark pattern, called nagging, can wear people down, says Burkell.
"Eventually people are just going to give in and say, 'Oh fine, I'll buy it.'"
It’s a tactic that works, says Arocena.
"If it was on my cart, chances are I was somewhat ready to check out … so that price drop ultimately convinces me to move forward with the purchase."
Gamification
Another design tactic to watch for: games on shopping sites that can keep consumers locked in to the site.

While browsing on Shein, the Marketplace team spotted an animated promotion that offered the chance to grab three free items: an iPhone Duo, an iPhone Max and a pair of AirPods Max. The chance to win didn’t come until about a week later but the prizes were first come, first serve and the stock was limited to one of each.
Fritsch says the game keeps consumers in the habit of visiting the site and "captured as a customer."

In an email, a Shein spokesperson said the company "is committed to complying with applicable laws and regulations in the markets where we operate." They added that they provide a transparent shopping experience and regularly review features on their platform as well as identify opportunities to improve customers’ shopping experience.
Confirmation shaming

On a "spin to win" game on Temu, the Marketplace team got a $350 credit. Although the game said they were just one step away from claiming it, they didn’t manage to get the credit, despite making multiple purchases.
When the Marketplace team left the app, a message said "Cancel your account rewards?" The options were "Stay and withdraw" or "I don't want cash."
Fritsch says that language is called confirmation shaming, which manipulates a consumer's emotions.

"The idea here is that a consumer has made a choice and they want to exercise that choice. And then at the last step, the vendor says, ‘Whoa, whoa, whoa, are you sure you wanna do this? You're walking away from all this potential money.'"
A message on Temu’s app that appeared when trying to leave a game saying 'I don’t want cash.' (CBC)

A Temu spokesperson said in a statement that "the interactive elements in our app are intended to make shopping more engaging and give users opportunities to unlock additional discounts. Users have a choice: they can shop without playing games, close a game and return to shopping, and turn off game-related notifications in the app’s settings."

In response to the repeated notifications, the company said users can unsubscribe from texts and email promotions. They added that they "listen to customer feedback ... and continue to refine platform features."
Possible solution?
In the European Union, lawmakers are making a push to specifically ban dark patterns through their Digital Services Act.

Marketplace checked out some of the same shopping sites using a VPN set to Sweden and found some differences. For example, on Amazon, free shipping was the pre-selected option, rather than paid shipping. Temu didn’t send emails after items were left in the cart. And coupons on Shein actually seemed to expire. (Walmart does not operate in Europe.)

"This is precisely what our services are monitoring," said Thomas Regnier, spokesperson on digital tech sovereignty for the European Commission. He said the differences between the North American and European shopping experiences on these sites show that the approach in the EU is working.
Even so, the European Commission wants to strengthen consumer protection further through the Digital Fairness Act.
"We need to reach that level where the Wild West is completely over in the online world, where platforms operate in a regulated environment, just like shops do in real life," said Regnier.
Thomas Regnier, spokesperson on digital tech sovereignty for the European Commission. (Fernando Moreno/CBC)
